The T20 Impact Index

Introduction

Who is the greatest T20 batter of all time? Fans argue with their hearts, often pointing to raw run totals or highlight-reel sixes. As data scientists, we wanted to settle the debate mathematically.

To find the true GOAT, we built a Composite Impact Score. It is designed to penalise slow, outdated anchors and reckless sloggers, and to reward only those who maximise both consistency and aggression.

\[ \text{Impact Score} = \frac{\text{Batting Average} \times \text{Strike Rate}}{100} \]

Fair fight rules. To keep weak opposition from skewing the numbers, we analyse only players from Full Member Test-playing nations with at least 50 T20I innings.

Fetching & Cleaning the Data

We pull career T20I batting data with the cricketdata package. The raw download is saved next to this file (t20_career_batting.rds), so re-rendering is instant and works offline. Delete that file to fetch fresh numbers.

Show code 
library(cricketdata)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)

cache_file <- "t20_career_batting.rds"
if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  raw <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  raw <- fetch_cricinfo(matchtype = "t20", sex = "men",
                        activity = "batting", type = "career")
  saveRDS(raw, cache_file)
}

# Be tolerant of older column names, then fail early with a clear message
raw <- raw %>% rename(any_of(c(Average = "Ave", StrikeRate = "SR")))
required <- c("Player", "Country", "Innings", "NotOuts", "Runs",
              "Average", "StrikeRate", "Fours", "Sixes")
absent <- setdiff(required, names(raw))
if (length(absent)) stop("cricketdata is missing columns: ", paste(absent, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)

# Full Member nations (full names or the short codes Cricinfo sometimes uses).
# Multi-country players such as "Eng/Ire" match too.
full_member <- regex(
  paste0("\\b(India|Ind|Australia|Aus|England|Eng|Pakistan|Pak|South Africa|SA|",
         "New Zealand|NZ|Sri Lanka|SL|West Indies|WI|Bangladesh|Ban|",
         "Afghanistan|Afg|Zimbabwe|Zim|Ireland|Ire)\\b"),
  ignore_case = TRUE
)

clean_data <- raw %>%
  filter(str_detect(Country, full_member), Innings >= 50) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Fours), !is.na(Sixes)) %>%          # missing is not the same as zero
  mutate(
    NotOuts       = coalesce(NotOuts, 0),
    Boundary_Runs = Fours * 4 + Sixes * 6,
    Boundary_Pct  = Boundary_Runs / Runs * 100,     # share of runs from 4s and 6s
    Impact_Score  = Average * StrikeRate / 100,     # the Impact Score
    NotOut_Pct    = NotOuts / Innings * 100         # finishing ability
  ) %>%
  filter(Boundary_Pct <= 100, !is.na(Impact_Score))  # drop impossible rows
Show code 
# A dark, saffron-accented ggplot theme shared by every chart
pal <- list(saffron = "#FF9933", amber = "#FFB347", deep = "#FF6A00", teal = "#2dd4bf",
            bg = "#11151c", ink = "#e6edf3", muted = "#8b949e", grid = "#222a35")

theme_saffron <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background   = element_rect(fill = pal$bg, colour = NA),
      panel.background  = element_rect(fill = pal$bg, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major  = element_line(colour = pal$grid, linewidth = 0.4),
      panel.grid.minor  = element_blank(),
      text              = element_text(colour = pal$ink),
      axis.text         = element_text(colour = pal$ink),
      axis.title        = element_text(colour = pal$muted, face = "bold", size = base_size - 2),
      plot.title        = element_text(colour = pal$saffron, face = "bold", size = base_size + 5,
                                       hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 4)),
      plot.subtitle     = element_text(colour = pal$muted, size = base_size - 1.5,
                                       hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 14)),
      plot.caption      = element_text(colour = pal$muted, size = base_size - 4,
                                       hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 12)),
      plot.title.position   = "plot",
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.title      = element_text(colour = pal$muted, size = base_size - 3),
      legend.text       = element_text(colour = pal$ink, size = base_size - 3),
      plot.margin       = margin(18, 22, 14, 18)
    )
}
theme_set(theme_saffron())

cap <- "Data: ESPNcricinfo via {cricketdata} | Min. 50 innings, Full Member nations | Analysis Before Wicket"
Show code 
# Everything the narrative below quotes comes from here, so the text can never drift from the charts
goat      <- slice_max(clean_data, Impact_Score, n = 1,  with_ties = FALSE)
top_15    <- slice_max(clean_data, Impact_Score, n = 15, with_ties = FALSE)
finisher  <- slice_max(top_15, NotOut_Pct, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

top_40 <- slice_max(clean_data, Impact_Score, n = 40, with_ties = FALSE)
mx <- mean(top_40$Boundary_Pct)
my <- mean(top_40$Impact_Score)
top_40 <- top_40 %>%
  mutate(Camp = case_when(
    Impact_Score >= my & Boundary_Pct >= mx ~ "Elite Enforcer",
    Impact_Score >= my                      ~ "Elite Anchor",
    TRUE                                    ~ "Chasing pack"))
anchor   <- top_40 %>% filter(Camp == "Elite Anchor")   %>% slice_max(Impact_Score, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
enforcer <- top_40 %>% filter(Camp == "Elite Enforcer") %>% slice_max(Impact_Score, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

fastest      <- slice_max(clean_data, StrikeRate,   n = 1,  with_ties = FALSE)
top_boundary <- slice_max(clean_data, Boundary_Pct, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)
med_boundary <- median(clean_data$Boundary_Pct)

1. The Ultimate Impact Index

Here are the top 15 players by Impact Score. The brightness of each bar shows their Finishing Ability: the percentage of innings they ended not out.

Show code 
ggplot(top_15, aes(x = fct_reorder(Player, Impact_Score), y = Impact_Score, fill = NotOut_Pct)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", Impact_Score)),
            hjust = -0.25, size = 4, fontface = "bold", colour = pal$ink) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#8a5a22", high = pal$amber, name = "Finishing ability\n(not-out %)") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "The Ultimate T20I Impact Index",
       subtitle = "Impact = (Batting Average x Strike Rate) / 100  |  Top 15",
       x = NULL, y = "Impact Score", caption = cap) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

The Verdict: the mathematical champion is V Kohli (India), with an Impact Score of 66.7. Notice the difference in style among the top 15: some reach their score through explosive hitting, while the brightest bar belongs to NT Tilak Varma , who finished not out in 37% of his innings.

2. The Anatomy of a T20 Batter

To see how players earn their Impact Scores, we plot Average (consistency) against Strike Rate (aggression). Bubble size is career runs, and colour is Boundary Dependency, from teal (rotates the strike) to saffron (lives off 4s and 6s). The dashed curves are lines of equal Impact Score.

Show code 
xr <- range(clean_data$Average)    + c(-2, 2)
yr <- range(clean_data$StrikeRate) + c(-3, 3)

# Lines of equal Impact Score: StrikeRate = 100 * k / Average
iso <- expand_grid(k = c(40, 50, 60), Average = seq(xr[1], xr[2], length.out = 300)) %>%
  mutate(StrikeRate = 100 * k / Average) %>%
  filter(StrikeRate >= yr[1], StrikeRate <= yr[2])
iso_lab <- iso %>% group_by(k) %>% slice_max(Average, n = 1) %>% ungroup()

ggplot(clean_data, aes(x = Average, y = StrikeRate)) +
  geom_line(data = iso, aes(group = k), colour = "#3b4452", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = iso_lab, aes(label = paste("Impact", k)),
            colour = "#6e7681", size = 3, hjust = 1, vjust = -0.6, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_point(aes(size = Runs, fill = Boundary_Pct),
             shape = 21, colour = pal$bg, stroke = 0.5, alpha = 0.92) +
  geom_text_repel(data = slice_max(clean_data, Impact_Score, n = 12, with_ties = FALSE),
                  aes(label = Player), colour = pal$ink, size = 3.4, fontface = "bold",
                  segment.colour = "#3b4452", box.padding = 0.5, min.segment.length = 0,
                  max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 7) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = pal$teal, high = pal$saffron, name = "Boundary\ndependency (%)") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2.5, 9), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = xr, ylim = yr) +
  labs(title = "The Anatomy of a T20 Batter",
       subtitle = "Average vs Strike Rate  |  bubble size = career runs",
       x = "Batting average (consistency)", y = "Strike rate (aggression)", caption = cap)

Reading the chart: the top-right is where the elite live, with a high average and a high strike rate. The bottom-right holds the classic anchors, who are consistent but at a slower tempo. The top-left holds the hitters who go big but are dismissed more often.

3. The Elite Quadrant

Now isolate the top 40 and map Impact Score against Boundary Dependency. The dashed lines mark the averages of this elite group.

Show code 
ggplot(top_40, aes(x = Boundary_Pct, y = Impact_Score)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = mx, ymin = my, ymax = Inf, fill = pal$teal,    alpha = 0.06) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = mx,   xmax = Inf, ymin = my, ymax = Inf, fill = pal$saffron, alpha = 0.06) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mx, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#4a5361") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = my, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#4a5361") +
  annotate("text", x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = "ELITE ANCHORS",   hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.7,
           colour = pal$teal,    fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  annotate("text", x = Inf,  y = Inf, label = "ELITE ENFORCERS", hjust = 1.1,  vjust = 1.7,
           colour = pal$saffron, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Camp), size = 4.5, alpha = 0.95) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = Player), colour = pal$ink, size = 3.2, fontface = "bold",
                  segment.colour = "#3b4452", box.padding = 0.35, max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Elite Enforcer" = pal$saffron,
                                 "Elite Anchor"   = pal$teal,
                                 "Chasing pack"   = "#6e7681"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The Elite Quadrant",
       subtitle = "Top 40 by Impact Score  |  top-left: anchors, top-right: enforcers",
       x = "Boundary dependency (% of runs from 4s and 6s)", y = "Composite Impact Score",
       caption = cap) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left")

The Takeaway: the top of the chart is where GOATs live, and there are two ways to get there. The anchors, led by V Kohli (Impact 66.7), earn their score through volume and consistency. The enforcers, led by Abhishek Sharma (Impact 64.5), earn it through boundary power.

4. The Pure Enforcers

Finally, the players who score the highest share of their runs purely through 4s and 6s. The dashed line is the median batter in our sample.

Show code 
ggplot(top_boundary, aes(x = fct_reorder(Player, Boundary_Pct), y = Boundary_Pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal$deep, width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = med_boundary, linetype = "dashed", colour = pal$muted) +
  annotate("text", x = 10.75, y = med_boundary, hjust = -0.06, colour = pal$muted, size = 3.4,
           label = sprintf("median batter: %.0f%%", med_boundary)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", Boundary_Pct)),
            hjust = -0.2, size = 4, fontface = "bold", colour = pal$ink) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1.2))) +   # headroom for the median label
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)), labels = label_percent(scale = 1, accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Most Boundary-Dependent Batters",
       subtitle = "Share of career runs scored in fours and sixes",
       x = NULL, y = "Boundary dependency", caption = cap) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

Conclusion

The data says the T20 GOAT debate is a fork in the road, and V Kohli sits at the top of the Impact Index. If you value pure consistency and finishing games, the elite anchors like V Kohli are your answer. If you want pure firepower, the explosive camp is led by Abhishek Sharma , and the most boundary-reliant batter in the sample is Abhishek Sharma , who scores 80% of his runs in fours and sixes.

One thing is certain: if you can’t balance your Average and Strike Rate, you won’t survive at the top of the Impact Index.

NoteMethod notes and limits
  • Impact Score is a simple product, Average x Strike Rate / 100. It does not adjust for era, pitch, batting position or opposition quality.
  • Not-outs inflate averages, so finishers get a small boost by construction.
  • Boundary Dependency is (4s x 4 + 6s x 6) / runs. Players with missing 4s/6s counts were dropped instead of being treated as zero.
  • All figures are career totals as of the cached download, so they say nothing about current form.
Data: ESPNcricinfo via the cricketdata package · Analysis Before Wicket
